name: BM_halin_reconstruction_infinite_hypomorphic_mutual_subgraph
title: Halin's conjecture on hypomorphic infinite graphs
statement_text: If two infinite graphs are hypomorphic, then each is isomorphic to a subgraph of the other.
context_text: Two graphs $G$ and $H$ are hypomorphic if there is a bijection $\varphi\colon V(G)\to V(H)$ with $G - v \cong H - \varphi(v)$ for every vertex $v$. For finite graphs the Reconstruction Conjecture asserts that hypomorphic simple graphs on at least three vertices are isomorphic. This fails for infinite graphs: the book shows that the infinite tree $T_\infty$ in which every vertex has countably infinite degree and the forest $2T_\infty$ consisting of two disjoint copies of $T_\infty$ are hypomorphic but not isomorphic (each is, however, isomorphic to a subgraph of the other). Halin's conjecture is the natural weakening of reconstruction for infinite graphs.
notes: Bowler, Erde, Heinig, Lehner and Pitz, 'A counterexample to the reconstruction conjecture for locally finite trees' (Bull. London Math. Soc. 49, 2017), state that their construction also answers a question of Halin; the status review should check whether it is this one.

name: BM_barat_thomassen_tree_decomposition_edge_connected
title: Barát–Thomassen conjecture
statement_text: For every tree $T$ there exists a natural number $k := k(T)$ such that every simple $k$-edge-connected graph whose number of edges is divisible by $e(T)$ admits a decomposition into copies of $T$.
context_text: A decomposition of a graph $G$ is a family of edge-disjoint subgraphs of $G$ whose union is $G$, so that every edge lies in exactly one member; a decomposition into copies of $T$ is one in which every member is isomorphic to $T$. Here $e(T)$ denotes the number of edges of $T$, and a graph is $k$-edge-connected if it has no edge cut with fewer than $k$ edges (in particular it is connected). The divisibility condition is obviously necessary, and some edge-connectivity is needed. As illustrations of the case where $T$ is a short path, the book shows that every connected graph with an even number of edges admits a decomposition into paths of length $2$, and that every $2$-connected $3$-regular graph on at least four vertices admits a decomposition into paths of length $3$.

related.note: Bensmail, Harutyunyan, Le and Thomassé propose a refinement of this conjecture

notes: Editorial lead, to be confirmed by the status review: Bensmail, Harutyunyan, Le, Merker and Thomassé, 'A proof of the Barát–Thomassen conjecture', J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 124 (2017).

name: BM_bridgeless_cycle_double_cover_small_bondy
title: Bondy's small cycle double cover conjecture
statement_text: Every simple graph on $n$ vertices without cut edges has a cycle double cover consisting of at most $n - 1$ cycles.
context_text: A cycle double cover of a graph is a family of cycles such that every edge lies in exactly two of them; a cut edge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of components, and a graph with a cut edge has no cycle double cover. The Cycle Double Cover Conjecture asserts that every graph without cut edges has a cycle double cover; Bondy's conjecture strengthens it for simple graphs. Since the cycles of a double cover have total length $2m$ and each has length at most $n$, a cycle double cover has at least $2m/n$ cycles (the average degree), so the complete graph $K_n$ needs at least $n-1$ cycles; the book calls a cycle double cover with at most $n-1$ cycles a small cycle double cover, and the conjecture says every simple graph without cut edges has one.

name: BM_bridgeless_cycle_double_cover_5_cycles
title: Five cycle double cover conjecture
statement_text: Every 2-edge-connected graph has a double cover by at most five even subgraphs.
context_text: In the book an even subgraph of $G$ is a spanning subgraph in which every vertex has even degree (equivalently, an edge-disjoint union of cycles, identified with its edge set); a double cover of $G$ is a family of subgraphs such that every edge lies in exactly two of them. A graph with a cut edge has no such cover, hence the hypothesis. The number five would be best possible: the book shows that the Petersen graph has no double cover by four even subgraphs, while it has a double cover by five. The conjecture strengthens the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture, since each even subgraph decomposes into cycles. Also attributed to Celmins (1984).

related.note: stronger form (prescribed cycle in the cover)
weaker: no bound on the number of even subgraphs

name: BM_linear_arboricity_regular_graphs
title: Linear arboricity conjecture
statement_text: Every simple $k$-regular graph has linear arboricity $\lceil (k+1)/2 \rceil$.
context_text: A linear forest is a graph each of whose components is a path, and the linear arboricity $\mathrm{la}(G)$ is the least number of linear forests into which the edge set of $G$ can be decomposed. For a $k$-regular graph the lower bound $\mathrm{la}(G) \ge \lceil (k+1)/2 \rceil$ follows by counting edges (a linear forest has at most $n-1$ edges), so the conjecture asks for the matching upper bound. Equivalently, every simple graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ satisfies $\mathrm{la}(G) \le \lceil (\Delta+1)/2 \rceil$. Using the Local Lemma, the book proves Alon's result that $\mathrm{la}(G) = r+1$ for every simple $2r$-regular graph of girth at least $2e(4r-2)$.
attributed_to: J. Akiyama, G. Exoo and F. Harary (1981); A.J.W. Hilton (1982)

name: BM_cubic_second_hamilton_cycle_polynomial
title: Finding a second Hamilton cycle in a cubic graph
statement_text: Is the following problem in $\mathsf{P}$? Given a cubic graph $G$ and a Hamilton cycle in $G$, find a second Hamilton cycle in $G$.
context_text: By Smith's theorem every edge of a cubic graph lies in an even number of Hamilton cycles, so a second Hamilton cycle always exists; the question is whether one can be found in polynomial time.

related.note: existence of a second Hamilton cycle in regular graphs

name: BM_k_disjoint_odd_paths_conp
title: Internally disjoint odd paths: is it in co-NP?
statement_text: Is the following problem in $\mathsf{co\text{-}NP}$? Given a graph $G$ and two $k$-subsets $X$ and $Y$ of $V(G)$, decide whether there exist $k$ internally disjoint $(X,Y)$-paths of odd length in $G$.
context_text: For subsets $X$ and $Y$ of $V(G)$, an $(X,Y)$-path is a path that starts at a vertex of $X$, ends at a vertex of $Y$, and whose internal vertices belong to neither $X$ nor $Y$; paths are internally disjoint if they have no internal vertex in common, a $k$-subset is a set of $k$ vertices, and the length of a path is its number of edges. Membership in $\mathsf{co\text{-}NP}$ means that whenever the answer is no there is a certificate of this fact checkable in polynomial time, i.e. a good characterisation of the graphs without such paths. Without the parity condition the problem is solvable in polynomial time by flow methods (Menger's theorem); the question is whether requiring all paths to have odd length still allows such a characterisation.

name: BM_thomassen_spanning_k_connected_bipartite_subgraph
title: Thomassen's spanning k-connected bipartite subgraph conjecture
statement_text: Every $2k$-connected digraph contains a spanning $k$-connected oriented subgraph.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and $D - S$ is strongly connected for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices. An oriented graph is a digraph without loops, multiple arcs or pairs of opposite arcs (an orientation of a simple graph); a spanning oriented subgraph of $D$ keeps all vertices of $D$ and, of each pair of opposite arcs, at most one. The conjecture thus asks that one can delete arcs from a $2k$-connected digraph so as to destroy all pairs of opposite arcs while keeping all vertices and $k$-connectivity. Applied to the symmetric digraph of a $2k$-connected graph it would give a $k$-connected orientation of that graph; it is a vertex-connectivity analogue of Nash-Williams' theorem, proved in the book, that every $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected orientation.
notes: The statement follows the book (French edition): « Tout graphe orienté 2k-connexe contient un sous-graphe orienté simple k-connexe couvrant », i.e. the Jackson–Thomassen conjecture on spanning k-connected oriented subgraphs of digraphs. The record's name and title keep the earlier reading (Thomassen's 1989 question on spanning k-connected bipartite subgraphs of undirected graphs, as cited by Delcourt–Ferber 2015), which is a different problem.

name: BM_bridgeless_cycle_double_cover_orientable_5
title: Orientable five cycle double cover conjecture
statement_text: Every 2-edge-connected graph has an orientable double cover by five even subgraphs.
context_text: A cycle double cover of a graph is orientable if its cycles can be oriented as directed cycles that together traverse every edge once in each direction; a double cover by even subgraphs (spanning subgraphs with all degrees even) is orientable if its members can be decomposed into cycles forming an orientable cycle double cover. This conjecture strengthens both the five cycle double cover conjecture (every 2-edge-connected graph has a double cover by at most five even subgraphs) and the orientable cycle double cover conjecture. By a theorem of Jaeger proved in the book, a graph with an orientable double cover by $k$ even subgraphs has a $k$-flow, so the conjecture also implies Tutte's 5-Flow Conjecture.

name: BM_kelmans_seymour_5_connected_nonplanar_k5_subdivision
title: Kelmans–Seymour conjecture
statement_text: Every 5-connected non-planar graph contains a subdivision of $K_5$.
context_text: A subdivision of $K_5$ is a graph obtained from $K_5$ by replacing its edges by internally disjoint paths. By Kuratowski's theorem every non-planar graph contains a subdivision of $K_5$ or of $K_{3,3}$; the conjecture says that under $5$-connectivity a subdivision of $K_5$ can always be found. For minors the corresponding statement is known with weaker connectivity: Wagner (1936) showed that every $4$-connected non-planar graph has a $K_5$-minor.
notes: Editorial lead, to be confirmed by the status review: He, Wang and Yu, 'The Kelmans–Seymour conjecture I–IV', J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 144 (2020).

name: BM_conway_thrackle_edges_at_most_vertices
title: Conway's thrackle conjecture
statement_text: No graph with more edges than vertices has a thrackle drawing.
context_text: A thrackle is a graph drawn in the plane in such a way that any two edges meet exactly once, either at a common end or at a crossing; such a drawing is called a thrackle embedding (or thrackle drawing). The book shows that every tree has a thrackle embedding, that the $4$-cycle has none, and that the triangle and all cycles of length $5$ or more have one. The conjecture says that a thrackleable graph has at most as many edges as vertices.

name: BM_harborth_planar_integer_length_straight_line_drawing
title: Harborth's conjecture (integral straight-line drawings)
statement_text: Every simple planar graph admits a straight-line planar embedding in which every edge has integer length.
context_text: A straight-line (rectilinear) planar embedding of a planar graph is a planar embedding in which every edge is drawn as a straight-line segment; by Fáry's theorem every simple planar graph has one. The conjecture asks that the vertices can moreover be placed so that the Euclidean length of every edge is an integer.

name: BM_erdos_sos_trees_edge_bound
title: Erdős–Sós conjecture
statement_text: If $G$ is a simple graph on $n$ vertices with $m > n(k-1)/2$ edges, then $G$ contains every tree with $k$ edges.
context_text: Here $n$ and $m$ denote the numbers of vertices and edges of the simple graph $G$, so the hypothesis says that $G$ has average degree greater than $k-1$, and 'contains' means contains as a subgraph (not necessarily induced). The bound is best possible, since a disjoint union of copies of $K_k$ has exactly $n(k-1)/2$ edges and no tree with $k$ edges (which has $k+1$ vertices). The book shows that a simple graph of minimum degree $k$ contains every tree with $k$ edges, and deduces that average degree at least $2(k-1)$ suffices.

name: BM_even_cycle_turan_number_lower_bound
title: Even-cycle Turán number
statement_text: For every $k \ge 2$ there is a positive constant $c$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k}) \ge c\, n^{1+1/k}$.
context_text: $\mathrm{ex}(n, C_{2k})$ is the maximum number of edges of a simple graph on $n$ vertices with no cycle of length $2k$; the Bondy–Simonovits theorem gives the matching upper bound $O(n^{1+1/k})$. Known for $k = 2, 3, 5$.

name: BM_diagonal_ramsey_constructive_exponential_lower_bound
title: Constructive exponential lower bound for diagonal Ramsey numbers
statement_text: Give a constructive proof that $r(k,k) \ge c^k$ for some constant $c > 1$ and all $k \ge 1$.
context_text: Erdős's 1947 probabilistic argument gives $r(k,k) \ge 2^{k/2}$ non-constructively.

name: BM_diagonal_ramsey_kth_root_limit
title: Limit of $r(k,k)^{1/k}$
statement_text: Does $\lim_{k\to\infty} r(k,k)^{1/k}$ exist? If so, determine its value.
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(k,k)$ is the least integer $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a clique of $k$ vertices or a stable set of $k$ vertices. The book proves $r(k,\ell) \le \binom{k+\ell-2}{k-1}$, hence $r(k,k) \le 4^{k-1}$, and Erdős's probabilistic lower bound $r(k,k) \ge 2^{k/2}$, so $\sqrt{2} \le \liminf_k r(k,k)^{1/k} \le \limsup_k r(k,k)^{1/k} \le 4$; the question is whether these two coincide and what the common value is.

name: BM_burr_erdos_tree_ramsey_2n_minus_2
title: Burr–Erdős tree Ramsey conjecture
statement_text: For every tree $T$ on $n$ vertices, $r(T,T) \le 2n - 2$.
context_text: For a graph $T$, the Ramsey number $r(T,T)$ is the least integer $N$ such that in every colouring of the edges of $K_N$ with two colours there is a monochromatic copy of $T$ (equivalently, every graph on $N$ vertices or its complement contains $T$ as a subgraph). The bound $2n-2$ is attained, for instance, by the star $K_{1,n-1}$ when $n$ is even. The conjecture would follow from the Erdős–Sós conjecture (applied to the colour class with more edges in a colouring of $K_{2n-2}$).

name: BM_hadwiger_minor_chromatic
title: Hadwiger's conjecture
statement_text: Every $k$-chromatic graph has a $K_k$-minor.
context_text: Known for $k \le 6$: the case $k = 5$ is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem (Wagner 1937) and $k = 6$ was settled by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (1993).

name: BM_hajos_k5_k6_subdivision_chromatic
title: Hajós conjecture for $k = 5$ and $k = 6$
statement_text: Does every $k$-chromatic graph contain a subdivision of $K_k$ when $k = 5$ and when $k = 6$?
context_text: Hajós conjectured this for all $k$; it holds for $k \le 4$ (Dirac 1952) and Catlin (1979) disproved it for every $k \ge 7$.

name: BM_erdos_lovasz_tihany_disjoint_chromatic_split
title: Erdős–Lovász Tihany conjecture
statement_text: Let $G$ be a $k$-chromatic graph containing no $k$-clique, and let $k + 1 = k_1 + k_2$ with $k_1, k_2 \ge 2$. Then $G$ has vertex-disjoint subgraphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ such that $G_i$ is $k_i$-chromatic, $i = 1, 2$.
context_text: A graph is $k$-chromatic if its chromatic number is $k$, and a $k$-clique is a set of $k$ pairwise adjacent vertices; the subgraphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ are required to be vertex-disjoint. The hypothesis excludes $K_k$, which has fewer than $k_1 + k_2 = k+1$ vertices and so cannot contain two such disjoint subgraphs; splitting a $k$-clique would only give $k_1 + k_2 = k$. The book proves the case where $G$ has no stable set of three vertices and $k \ge 3$ (Lovász and Seymour).

name: BM_el_zahar_erdos_induced_disjoint_union
title: El-Zahar–Erdős conjecture
statement_text: Does there exist a function $f$ such that every graph of chromatic number at least $f(r,k)$ contains either an $r$-clique or an induced subgraph which is the disjoint union of two $k$-chromatic graphs?
context_text: An $r$-clique is a set of $r$ pairwise adjacent vertices and a graph is $k$-chromatic if its chromatic number is $k$. The second alternative asks for two vertex-disjoint subgraphs $G_1$, $G_2$ of chromatic number $k$ with no edge of $G$ between them, such that $G[V(G_1) \cup V(G_2)]$ is exactly their disjoint union. The question is whether large chromatic number forces, in the absence of a large clique, two 'independent' highly chromatic induced pieces.

name: BM_gyarfas_triangle_free_infinite_chromatic_induced_trees
title: Gyárfás's tree conjecture for triangle-free graphs
statement_text: Every triangle-free graph of infinite chromatic number contains every finite tree as an induced subgraph.
context_text: It would follow from the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, which asserts that for every tree $T$ there is a function $f_T$ such that $\chi(G) \le f_T(\omega(G))$ for every graph $G$ with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $T$: a triangle-free graph ($\omega \le 2$) without an induced copy of $T$ would then have all its finite subgraphs of chromatic number at most $f_T(2)$, hence, by the de Bruijn–Erdős compactness theorem, finite chromatic number. The infinite formulation is equivalent to saying that triangle-free graphs of sufficiently large finite chromatic number contain any given tree as an induced subgraph.

name: BM_albertson_toroidal_delete_3_vertices_4_colorable
title: Albertson's toroidal colouring conjecture
statement_text: Every toroidal graph has three vertices whose deletion leaves a 4-colourable graph.
context_text: A toroidal graph is one that can be embedded on the torus. The book reports that Albertson conjectured more generally that for every surface $\Sigma$ there is an integer $f(\Sigma)$ such that all but $f(\Sigma)$ vertices of any graph embeddable on $\Sigma$ can be $4$-coloured, the torus case being $f = 3$ (three is needed since $K_7$ embeds on the torus). Thomassen proved that there are exactly four $6$-critical graphs on the torus and deduced that all but two vertices of a toroidal graph can be $5$-coloured; Albertson and Hutchinson showed that a graph embeddable on the sphere with $k$ handles becomes planar after deleting at most $k\sqrt{2n}$ vertices.

name: BM_hadwiger_nelson_plane_unit_distance_chromatic
title: Chromatic number of the plane (Hadwiger–Nelson problem)
statement_text: Determine the chromatic number of the unit-distance graph of the plane, i.e. the least number of colours needed to colour the points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ so that no two points at distance $1$ receive the same colour.
context_text: The unit-distance graph of the plane has all points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ as vertices, two points being adjacent if they are at distance exactly $1$. The book shows that the Hajós graph, which is $4$-chromatic, is a unit-distance graph, giving $\chi \ge 4$, and that a $7$-colouring of the faces of a suitable hexagonal tiling gives $\chi \le 7$; at the time of the English edition (2008) these were the best known bounds, $4 \le \chi(\mathbb{R}^2) \le 7$.
notes: Editorial lead, to be confirmed by the status review: de Grey (2018) showed the chromatic number is at least 5.

name: BM_1_factorization_dense_regular_graphs
title: 1-factorization conjecture
statement_text: Every simple $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices with $n$ even and $d \ge n/2$ is $d$-edge-colourable.
context_text: Equivalently, such graphs have a 1-factorization. Usually stated (Chetwynd and Hilton 1985) with the sharper threshold $d \ge 2\lceil n/4 \rceil - 1$.
notes: Editorial lead, to be confirmed by the status review: Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus and Treglown, 'Proof of the 1-factorization and Hamilton decomposition conjectures', Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 244 (2016), for sufficiently large $n$.

name: BM_vizing_interchange_kempe_optimal_edge_coloring
title: Vizing's interchange conjecture
statement_text: Given a proper edge colouring of a graph $G$, a proper edge colouring of $G$ with $\chi'(G)$ colours can be obtained by a sequence of colour interchanges on alternating paths or cycles (Kempe changes).
context_text: $\chi'(G)$ is the chromatic index of $G$. Given a proper edge colouring with colour classes $M_1, M_2, \ldots$ and two distinct colours $i$ and $j$, every component of the subgraph formed by the edges coloured $i$ or $j$ is a path or an even cycle whose edges alternate between the two colours (an alternating path or cycle, the edge analogue of a Kempe chain); a colour interchange swaps $i$ and $j$ on one such component and yields another proper edge colouring. Such interchanges are the main tool in the book's proofs of König's and Vizing's edge-colouring theorems. The conjecture asserts that interchanges alone suffice to transform any proper edge colouring of $G$ into one using only $\chi'(G)$ colours.
notes: Editorial lead, to be confirmed by the status review: Narboni, 'Vizing's edge-recoloring conjecture holds' (arXiv:2302.12914, 2023); triangle-free case by Bonamy, Defrain, Klimošová, Lagoutte and Narboni (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 2023).

name: BM_kotzig_unique_k_path_nonexistence
title: Kotzig's unique $k$-path conjecture
statement_text: For $k \ge 3$ there is no graph in which every pair of vertices is connected by a unique path of length $k$.
context_text: The length of a path is its number of edges. For $k = 2$ the property says that any two vertices have exactly one common neighbour, and the Friendship Theorem, proved in the book, shows that the graphs with this property are exactly the windmills (triangles sharing a common vertex); Kotzig's conjecture asserts that for every $k \ge 3$ no graph has the property that each pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one path of length $k$.

name: BM_smith_longest_cycles_k_connected_intersection
title: Smith's conjecture on longest cycles
statement_text: In a $k$-connected graph, $k \ge 2$, any two longest cycles have at least $k$ vertices in common.
context_text: A longest cycle is a cycle of maximum length in the graph. The book proves the case $k = 2$: any two longest cycles in a connected loopless graph without cut vertex have at least two vertices in common. The conjecture asks for $k$ common vertices under $k$-connectivity. Attributed to S. Smith; see Grötschel (1984).

name: BM_bondy_cubic_cyclically_4_connected_long_cycle
title: Bondy's linear-length cycle conjecture for cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs
statement_text: There is a positive constant $c$ such that every 3-connected, cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph on $n$ vertices contains a cycle of length at least $cn$.
context_text: A graph is cyclically $k$-edge-connected if it has no edge cut with fewer than $k$ edges whose deletion leaves two components that each contain a cycle. The conjecture asserts that 3-connected cubic graphs that are moreover cyclically 4-edge-connected have cycles of length linear in the number of vertices. Attributed to J.A. Bondy; see Fleischner and Jackson (1989).

name: BM_birmele_long_cycles_pairwise_intersecting_hitting_set
title: Birmelé's conjecture on long cycles
statement_text: If any two cycles of length at least $k$ in a graph intersect, then the graph has a set of $k$ vertices meeting every cycle of length at least $k$.
context_text: Two cycles intersect if they have a common vertex, and the length of a cycle is its number of edges. The hypothesis is that the graph has no two vertex-disjoint cycles of length at least $k$; the conclusion is that some set of $k$ vertices meets (contains a vertex of) every cycle of length at least $k$. This is the case of packing number one of an Erdős–Pósa-type duality for long cycles.

related.note: Erdős–Pósa property for long cycles (directed version)

name: BM_caccetta_haggkvist_weighted_cycle
title: Weighted Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
statement_text: Let $D$ be a strongly connected digraph with a positive weight function $w$ on its arcs such that $w^-(v) \ge 1$ and $w^+(v) \ge 1$ for every vertex $v$. Then $D$ contains a directed cycle of weight at least $1$.
context_text: In this section of the book digraphs are strict, that is, without loops or multiple arcs. The arcs of $D$ carry positive real weights $w(a)$; $w^-(v)$ and $w^+(v)$ denote the total weight of the arcs entering and leaving $v$, and the weight of a directed cycle is the sum of the weights of its arcs. With all weights equal to $1/k$ the hypothesis says that every in- and out-degree is at least $k$. The book proves (Bollobás and Scott) the analogous statement for directed paths: if $w^+(v) \ge 1$ for all vertices $v$ but one, then $D$ has a directed path of weight at least $1$.

related.note: the unweighted case; this statement appears in its discussion

name: BM_matthews_sumner_4_connected_claw_free_hamiltonian
title: Matthews–Sumner conjecture
statement_text: Every 4-connected claw-free graph is Hamiltonian.
context_text: The claw is the complete bipartite graph $K_{1,3}$, and a graph is claw-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to the claw; every line graph is claw-free. The book outlines Ryjáček's closure: repeatedly adding an edge between two non-adjacent neighbours of a vertex whose neighbourhood induces a connected non-complete graph preserves Hamiltonicity and ends with the line graph of a triangle-free graph. Via this closure the conjecture is equivalent to Thomassen's conjecture that every 4-connected line graph is Hamiltonian.

name: BM_barnette_simple_4_polytopes_hamiltonian
title: Barnette's conjecture on 4-regular 4-polytopes
statement_text: The graph of every 4-regular 4-polytope (every simple 4-dimensional convex polytope) is Hamiltonian.
context_text: A $4$-polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of points of $\mathbb{R}^4$ not lying in a common hyperplane, and its graph has the vertices of the polytope as vertices and its $1$-dimensional faces (edges) as edges. The polytope is $4$-regular when its graph is $4$-regular, i.e. it is simple (every vertex lies in exactly four facets). The conjecture asserts that the graph of every such polytope has a Hamilton cycle. Attributed to D.W. Barnette; see Grünbaum (1970), p. 1145.

related.note: Barnette's better-known conjecture on cubic bipartite planar graphs

name: BM_cantoni_planar_cubic_three_hamilton_cycles_triangle
title: Cantoni's conjecture
statement_text: Every planar cubic graph with exactly three Hamilton cycles contains a triangle.
context_text: By Smith's theorem every edge of a cubic graph lies in an even number of Hamilton cycles, so a Hamiltonian cubic graph has at least three Hamilton cycles; the book shows that $K_4$ and the generalised Petersen graph $P_{2,9}$ have exactly three, and that for every $n \ge 2$ there is a simple cubic graph on $2n$ vertices with exactly three. The conjecture says that a planar cubic graph attaining this minimum must contain a triangle. Graphs are presumably simple here (the book's wording does not say so; the multigraph with two vertices and three parallel edges is a trivial exception). See also Ninčák (1974) and Tutte (1976).

name: BM_thomassen_vertex_transitive_finitely_many_non_hamiltonian
title: Thomassen's conjecture on Hamiltonian vertex-transitive graphs
statement_text: All but finitely many connected vertex-transitive graphs are Hamiltonian.
context_text: Only five connected vertex-transitive graphs without a Hamilton cycle are known: $K_2$, the Petersen graph, the Coxeter graph, and the truncations of the last two.

related.note: Lovász's Hamilton-path problem; discusses the known exceptions

name: BM_chvatal_toughness_k_tough_hamiltonian
title: Chvátal's toughness conjecture
statement_text: There exists a positive integer $k$ such that every $k$-tough graph is Hamiltonian.
context_text: A connected graph $G$ is $t$-tough if $c(G - S) \le |S|/t$ for every vertex cut $S$ of $G$, where $c(\cdot)$ denotes the number of components (complete graphs, having no vertex cut, are $t$-tough for all $t$). Every Hamiltonian graph is $1$-tough, but $1$-toughness does not suffice. The book presents a construction of Bauer, Broersma and Veldman of $2$-tough graphs that are not Hamiltonian, so the constant $k$ in Chvátal's conjecture, if it exists, is greater than $2$.

name: BM_hypohamiltonian_min_degree_4
title: Hypohamiltonian graphs of minimum degree at least 4
statement_text: Is there a hypohamiltonian graph of minimum degree at least $4$?
context_text: A graph is hypohamiltonian if it is not Hamiltonian but every vertex-deleted subgraph $G - v$ is Hamiltonian. The book shows that the Petersen graph is the smallest hypohamiltonian graph and that the Coxeter graph is also hypohamiltonian; both are cubic. The question is whether a hypohamiltonian graph can have all degrees at least $4$.

name: BM_grotschel_bipartite_hypotraceable_nonexistence
title: Grötschel's conjecture on bipartite hypotraceable graphs
statement_text: There is no bipartite hypotraceable graph.
context_text: A graph is hypotraceable if it has no Hamilton path but every vertex-deleted subgraph has one.
